author: high2
claim: Direct proof attempt for the forward implication: solved.
evidence: Assume G is bipartite with parts A and B. Every edge crosses between A and B. Therefore a traversal of a cycle alternates between A and B at every step. A return to the starting part, and hence to the starting vertex, can occur only after an even number of steps. Thus no odd cycle exists.

author: high2
claim: Direct proof attempt for the reverse implication: solved.
evidence: Lemma: every closed walk of odd length in a finite undirected graph contains a cycle of odd length. Indeed, among odd closed walks choose one W of minimum length. If a vertex other than the common initial/final vertex occurs twice in W, or the initial vertex occurs at an intermediate time, cut W at two consecutive occurrences of that repeated vertex. This gives two closed walks of positive lengths strictly smaller than the length of W, and their lengths sum to the odd length of W. Exactly one has odd length, contradicting minimality. Thus W has no repeated vertices except its equal initial and final vertices, so W itself is an odd cycle. Now assume G has no odd cycle. Hence every closed walk has even length. In each connected component choose a root r. For a vertex v, any two walks from r to v have the same parity: following the first and then the reverse of the second is a closed walk whose length is the sum of their lengths, and this sum is even. Put v in A if this common parity is even and in B if it is odd. If uv is an edge and P is a walk from r to u, then P followed by uv is a walk from r to v with the opposite parity. Hence every edge joins A to B. Combining these componentwise partitions makes G bipartite.

links.attempt_summary: The odd-closed-walk lemma makes root-to-vertex walk parity well-defined; edges flip parity, yielding a bipartition.

counterexample_search_for_stuck_subgoal.summary: Not needed because the subgoal was proved.

author: high
claim: Direct-plan subgoal 1 (solved): if a finite undirected graph is bipartite, then every cycle has even length.
evidence: Let the bipartition be A and B. On a cycle v_0 v_1 ... v_{m-1} v_0, consecutive vertices belong to opposite classes. Starting from v_0, induction around the cycle places v_i in the same class as v_0 exactly when i is even. The closing edge v_{m-1}v_0 therefore forces m-1 to be odd, hence m is even. Thus no odd cycle exists. Plan id: direct-two-implications; attempt type: direct; status: solved; no external result or computation used.

author: high
claim: Direct-plan subgoal 2 (solved): if a finite undirected graph has no odd cycle, then it is bipartite.
evidence: In each connected component choose a root r and let d(x) be shortest-path distance from r. Choose for every non-root x a parent p(x) with d(p(x))=d(x)-1. The parent edges form a rooted spanning tree T: parent iteration reaches r, and a cycle in T would have a maximum-level vertex with two lower-level neighbors although it has only one parent. If an original edge xy had endpoints whose distances have the same parity, the inequalities |d(x)-d(y)|<=1 force d(x)=d(y)=k. Such an edge is not in T. The unique T-path from x to y goes from level k to the deepest common ancestor level h and back to level k, so it has length 2(k-h). Together with xy it is a simple cycle of odd length 2(k-h)+1, contradiction. Hence every edge crosses between even and odd distance classes; taking their unions over all components gives a bipartition. Plan id: direct-two-implications; attempt type: direct; status: solved; no external result or computation used.

glossary.r: the chosen root of a connected component
glossary.y: the other endpoint of an edge
glossary.T: the rooted spanning tree of parent edges
glossary.h: the distance of the deepest common ancestor

author: high4
claim: The direct parity-coloring plan proves the complete target theorem.
evidence: First prove the internal lemma that every odd closed walk contains an odd cycle: induct on its length; an internally repetition-free closed walk is a cycle, while an internal repeated vertex splits the walk into two strictly shorter closed walks, one odd. If G has bipartition (U,V), every cycle alternates between U and V and hence is even. Conversely assume G has no odd cycle. The lemma implies that G has no odd closed walk. In each connected component choose a root. Two paths from the root to the same vertex cannot have opposite parity, since one followed by the reverse of the other would be an odd closed walk. Thus classify every vertex by the parity of any root path. If an edge joined two vertices of the same class, a root path to the first, that edge, and the reverse of a root path to the second would form an odd closed walk. Hence every edge crosses the two classes, giving a bipartition.

links.subgoal: Complete equivalence between bipartiteness and absence of odd cycles
links.attempt_summary: All three subgoals solved directly and assembled into a self-contained proof.

glossary.U: the first class of a bipartition of G
glossary.V: the second class of a bipartition of G

author: high3
claim: Direct proof subgoal solved: if G has no odd cycle, then G is bipartite.
evidence: For each connected component choose a rooted spanning tree T and color a vertex by the parity of its depth. If an edge uv had endpoints of the same parity, uv is not a tree edge. If w is the last common vertex on the root-to-u and root-to-v paths, then the unique tree u-v path has length d(u)+d(v)-2d(w), which is even. That simple tree path together with uv is then a cycle of odd length, a contradiction. Thus all edges cross the two parity classes; taking their unions over components gives a bipartition.

claim: Direct proof subgoal solved: if G contains no cycle of odd length, then G is bipartite.
evidence: For every component C choose a root r_C and let d_C(v) be the shortest-path distance from r_C to v. For each nonroot v choose a neighbor p(v) with d_C(p(v))=d_C(v)-1. These parent edges form a spanning tree T_C: parent iteration reaches the root, and a hypothetical cycle has a maximum-depth vertex whose two cycle neighbors would both have to be its unique parent. Partition all vertices according to even or odd d_C. If an edge uv had endpoints of the same parity, it could not be a parent edge. In T_C, let w be the last common vertex on the root-u and root-v paths. The unique u-v tree path has length d_C(u)+d_C(v)-2d_C(w), which is even; adjoining uv therefore gives a simple odd cycle, a contradiction. Hence every edge crosses the parity partition.

author: high7
claim: Solved direct subgoal: if a finite undirected graph contains no odd cycle, it is bipartite.
evidence: Work componentwise. In each connected component, construct a spanning tree by beginning with one root and repeatedly adjoining an edge from the vertices already reached to a vertex not yet reached; connectivity supplies such an edge and finiteness makes the process terminate. Color each vertex by parity of its distance from the root in the tree. Every tree edge crosses colors. If a non-tree edge had equally colored endpoints, the unique tree path between those endpoints would have even length, because colors alternate along tree edges. That path together with the non-tree edge is an odd cycle, contrary to hypothesis. Hence all graph edges cross colors, giving a bipartition. Isolated vertices may be placed in either class.

links.attempt_summary: A spanning forest supplies a depth-parity coloring; any monochromatic non-tree edge would close an odd fundamental cycle.

author: high5
claim: Solved subgoal: a finite undirected graph with no odd-length cycle is bipartite.
evidence: For every connected component H choose a rooted spanning tree T. Color a vertex by the parity of the length of its unique root path in T. For an edge xy, let Q be the unique tree path between x and y. The parity of the length of Q equals the parity of the sum of the two root-path lengths, because their common initial segment is counted twice. If x and y had equal colors, Q would have even length. Then xy is not the tree edge Q (whose length would be one), and Q together with xy is a simple cycle of odd length, contradiction. Therefore all edges cross the two color classes.
